1.pericope_label: Then all the captains of the forces, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the people from the least even unto the greatest, came near, and said unto Jeremiah the prophet, Let, we beseech thee, our supplication be accepted before thee, and pray for us unto the Lord thy God, that the Lord thy God may shew us the way wherein we may walk. Then Jeremiah said, I have heard you; whatsoever thing the Lord shall answer you, I will declare it unto you. Then they said, The Lord be a true and faithful witness between us

schools.summary: Places the halt near Bethlehem and summarises the whole transaction in advance, and adds the sharpest note in the tile on the ten days that passed before the answer came, rejecting the view that the delay was the prophet's own, waiting on a conviction matured by his meditation, since that rests on a denial of inspiration; reads the acceptance of the request as simple accession, and the position of the applicants as genuinely difficult and dangerous.

Holds that they acted more culpably in coming than if they had gone straight to Egypt, since they either dissembled or were so stupefied by hypocrisy as to lose their understanding, and generalises it into a rule about asking counsel with the matter already settled; explains the phrase about the Lord thy God as extolling the prophet rather than disowning God, an admission that recoiled on their own head, and notices that the oath was never asked for, so that swearing it of their own accord bound them twice over.

Allows the applicants more honesty than the others do, holding that they really did not know which way was safest and wished God's mind on the point though they inclined to Egypt, and takes the appeal to a witness at its word, since the Lord will register the covenant and bless or curse accordingly; the good or evil undertaken is glossed as what is grateful or ungrateful to us.

Reads the approach as calculated, the prophet sought out at length only to serve a turn and their coming near betraying how far off they had kept till then, and finds the words wonderfully well chosen, since men who had him under their command approach as petitioners in a way meant to persuade him to say what they wanted, while the phrase about the Lord thy God confesses that they were unworthy to call God their own.

positions.view: no: they acted more culpably in coming than if they had gone straight to Egypt, since they either dissembled or were stupefied by hypocrisy; nothing is more common than to deliberate about a thing already settled
no: they had set their faces toward Egypt already and wanted only the Lord's sanction
no: the prophet was sought out at length only to serve a turn, and their coming near betrays how far off they had kept till then
yes in part: they really did not know which way was safest and wished God's mind on the point, though they inclined to Egypt
yes: they turn to him acknowledging a true prophet and trusting his patriotism, in a position truly difficult and dangerous

debates.question: Why do they say the Lord thy God?

positions.view: a confession that they were unworthy to call God their own, made with a great opinion of the prophet's interest in heaven

not a disowning of God nor an exemption from his authority, but an extolling of the prophet as God's true and lawful messenger, which recoiled on their own head, since if he was God's prophet they ought to have obeyed at once

debates.question: What did they undertake to accept?

positions.view: not what is morally good or evil, since nothing morally evil can come from God, but what is agreeable or disagreeable, profitable or not, in their own esteem
whatever is grateful or ungrateful to us
the test of fidelity itself, since the one way to prove ourselves is to hold the word binding whether it pleases us or not, never murmuring as the ungodly do when a yoke is laid on them

outliers.reading: Adds a sharp note on the ten days that passed before the answer came, reporting two scholars who make the delay the prophet's own, waiting on a conviction matured by his own meditation, and rejecting that view as resting on a denial of divine inspiration.

Notices what the others pass over, that the prophet had not asked for an oath at all: they swore of their own accord, and so bound themselves twice over, since men who send for a prophet unasked can plead no excuse afterwards; and adds that nothing so confuses the mind and senses as hypocrisy, which alone makes men rush on to swear without dreading perjury.

themes: Then all the captains of the forces, and Johanan the son of Kareah, and Jezaniah the son of Hoshaiah, and all the people from the least even unto the greatest, came near,

And said unto Jeremiah the prophet, Let, we beseech thee, our supplication be accepted before thee, and pray for us unto the Lord thy God, even for all this remnant; (for we are left but a few of many, as thine eyes do behold us:)
That the Lord thy God may shew us the way wherein we may walk, and the thing that we may do.

Then Jeremiah the prophet said unto them, I have heard you; behold, I will pray unto the Lord your God according to your words; and it shall come to pass, that whatsoever thing the Lord shall answer you, I will declare it unto you; I will keep nothing back from you.
Then they said to Jeremiah, The Lord be a true and faithful witness between us, if we do not even according to all things for the which the Lord thy God shall send thee to us.
Whether it be good, or whether it be evil, we will obey the voice of the Lord our God, to whom we send thee; that it may be well with us, when we obey the voice of the Lord our God.

7.pericope_label: And it came to pass after ten days, that the word of the Lord came unto Jeremiah. Then called he Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the people, and said unto them, Thus saith the Lord, the God of Israel, unto whom ye sent me to present your supplication before him; If ye will still abide in this land, then will I build you, and not pull you down. Be not afraid of the king of Babylon, of whom ye are afraid: for I am with you to save you. And I will shew mercies unto you

schools.summary: Makes the ten days deliberate reticence, the prophet refusing an answer of his own on the spur of the moment and waiting in prayer until there came into his mind what he could utter as an oracle, and notices that the suspense sharpened the eagerness of the crowd; hears in the building and planting the formulae with which the prophet's work began, corrects the word for repenting to a change of purpose rather than regret, and divides the promise of return between a carrying to Babylon with later restoration and immediate leave for the remnant to go back each to his own field.

Distinguishes the case of a special question from a common rule of life to explain the delay, and finds the interval keeping ostentation out and making the people receive the word as God's; observes that a bare command would have sufficed but that God let himself down to their infirmity by giving counsel and testifying it would be for their good, takes the promised mercy of the king of Babylon as a heart God would turn, and marks how carefully the delivery was made to leaders and people alike.

Turns the delay into doctrine, that prophets could no more prophesy at will than the disciples could work miracles at will, both gifts hanging on the will of the Most High and given only for the moment, and has God satisfied with what the nation has already suffered and changing his providence for the rest.

Offers the same reasons for the delay and adds that it showed the prophet did not speak of himself nor when he chose, drawing the lesson that we should keep waiting on God for direction; supplies the comparison that gives the promise its force, since their brethren had been carried off, so those who may stay should count it mercy and duty and never quit that land while they can hold it.

debates.question: Why did the answer take ten days?

positions.view: that it might carry greater weight and appear no device of the prophet's own, and chiefly to mortify an impatient people whose hypocrisy God knew; the prophet did not spend the interval praying but laid the case before God and waited
perhaps to punish their hypocrisy, and to show that the prophet did not speak of himself nor when he chose; it teaches us to keep waiting on God for direction
because prophets could no more prophesy at will than the disciples could work miracles at will, both gifts hanging on the will of the Most High and given only for the moment
deliberate reticence: he would not answer on the spur of the moment but waited in prayer until there came into his mind what he could utter as an oracle, as an earlier prophet waited seven days
a special question required waiting where a common rule of life would not have, and the interval kept ostentation out and made the people receive the word as God's

debates.question: Who is to show the mercy promised?

positions.view: the king of Babylon, whose heart God would turn, since God shows mercies not only in forgiving but in inclining the hearts of men, and can make a father out of a savage wild beast
God obtains the compassion for them, so that the king shows pity

the question is rather what the promised return means, either a carrying to Babylon followed by restoration or immediate leave for the remnant to go back each to his own field, the second suiting the prophet's aim better

debates.question: What does the promise of building require of them?

positions.view: that they accept the punishment inflicted and stay as they are rather than seek safety in plans of their own devising; the word for repenting means a change of purpose from judgment to mercy, not regret
that they obey, the punishment having been inflicted for rebellion and to be arrested as soon as they obey
that they believe, since God let himself down to their infirmity by giving counsel instead of commanding, so their obstinacy added unbelief to contempt
that they value what they have, since their brethren were carried off and those who may stay should count it mercy and duty

outliers.reading: Marks how carefully the answer was delivered to leaders and people alike, so that neither could afterwards plead the other's compulsion, and notes that the prophet describes himself as presenting the people's own prayer, acting as a middle person between God and them and asking nothing for himself.

Observes that the answer was delivered publicly and faithfully as received, nothing kept back, according to the promise the prophet had given; and draws from the ten days the lesson that we should keep waiting on God for direction, the vision being for an appointed time.

themes: And it came to pass after ten days, that the word of the Lord came unto Jeremiah.
Then called he Johanan the son of Kareah, and all the captains of the forces which were with him, and all the people from the least even to the greatest,
And said unto them, Thus saith the Lord, the God of Israel, unto whom ye sent me to present your supplication before him;
If ye will still abide in this land, then will I build you, and not pull you down, and I will plant you, and not pluck you up: for I repent me of the evil that I have done unto you.
Be not afraid of the king of Babylon, of whom ye are afraid; be not afraid of him, saith the Lord: for I am with you to save you, and to deliver you from his hand.
And I will shew mercies unto you, that he may have mercy upon you, and cause you to return to your own land.

13.pericope_label: But if ye say, We will not dwell in this land, neither obey the voice of the Lord your God, saying, No; but we will go into the land of Egypt, where we shall see no war: then it shall come to pass, that the sword, which ye feared, shall overtake you there. Know certainly that I have admonished you this day. For ye dissembled in your hearts, when ye sent me unto the Lord your God. Now therefore know certainly that ye shall die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence

schools.summary: Sets out the structure of the conditional sentence and puts the irony plainly, that the very evil they feared at home would overtake them in Egypt; states the attraction of Egypt with some sympathy, since it was still the granary of the East and its harvests made a bright contrast to the famine they had known, suspects that a rush of fugitives from several nations was moving the same way, and asks how the prophet knew their hearts, whether by looks and whispers or by the intuition of inspiration.

Grounds the condemnation in the law, which had forbidden setting the heart on Egypt and been confirmed often by the prophets, so that even a lawful thing attempted against God's express will would be diabolical presumption; makes the address to a remnant a deliberate check on the inebriation of prosperity, prefers that they deceived themselves rather than the prophet, since he is not named in the clause, and notices that they meant not to settle in Egypt but to wait there until they might return against God's will.

Gives a reason for the prohibition that no one else gives, that God knew their propensity to idolatry would make them take up the worship of the country, keeps the threat short and physical, the sword and famine at their heels to overtake and destroy them, and closes in bewilderment that men so disposed took any trouble to inquire at all, unless out of curiosity and meaning to obey only if the answer fell in with their inclination.

debates.question: Why is the flight to Egypt condemned?

positions.view: the law had forbidden setting the heart on Egypt and the prophets had often confirmed it, so that even a lawful thing attempted against God's express will would be diabolical presumption; the root of the rebellion is a people who paid no regard to a favour freely promised
the prophet had resisted the thought of an Egyptian alliance from first to last, though the attraction was real, Egypt being still the granary of the East
because God knew their propensity to idolatry would make them take up the worship of the country
because the very evil they feared at home would overtake them there
the choices are laid out without being settled: the prophet, or their own souls, or deceit used to the hurt of their souls
themselves, since the prophet is not named in the clause and the ungodly who affect astuteness weave only snares for their own feet

nobody for long, since looks and whispers may have betrayed them, or the prophet read their secret counsels by the intuition of inspiration: they meant all along to act as they liked, with his approval if it could be had and without it if not
an incorrigible people in whom ingratitude, hypocrisy and rebellion seem enthroned

debates.question: Who exactly falls under the sentence?

positions.view: not everyone who went into Egypt but everyone obstinately set on going, since some were carried there against their will, the prophet and his scribe among them

possibly a wider company, since a rush of fugitives from several nations was looking to Egypt as its one hope; the warning gathers up the prophet's old familiar phrases, so that by rejecting his counsel they involve themselves in the worst evils he ever prophesied
those the sword and famine overtake at their heels, to destroy them there

outliers.reading: Adds the force of the example standing before their eyes, since the man who now threatens them had for years been the herald of a vengeance they had at last seen executed, which no other speaker could have said with the same authority; and makes the address to a remnant a deliberate check, since men in prosperity are in a manner inebriated and hard to rule, so that the reminder of their humble condition was meant to make them teachable.

Closes in bewilderment rather than analysis, confessing himself puzzled that men so disposed should trouble to inquire at all, unless out of curiosity, since they did not intend to obey and would follow the answer only if it fell in with their own inclination.

themes: But if ye say, We will not dwell in this land, neither obey the voice of the Lord your God,
Saying, No; but we will go into the land of Egypt, where we shall see no war, nor hear the sound of the trumpet, nor have hunger of bread; and there will we dwell:
And now therefore hear the word of the Lord, ye remnant of Judah; Thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; If ye wholly set your faces to enter into Egypt, and go to sojourn there;

Then it shall come to pass, that the sword, which ye feared, shall overtake you there in the land of Egypt, and the famine, whereof ye were afraid, shall follow close after you there in Egypt; and there ye shall die.

So shall it be with all the men that set their faces to go into Egypt to sojourn there; they shall die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence: and none of them shall remain or escape from the evil that I will bring upon them.

For thus saith the Lord of hosts, the God of Israel; As mine anger and my fury hath been poured forth upon the inhabitants of Jerusalem; so shall my fury be poured forth upon you, when ye shall enter into Egypt: and ye shall be an execration, and an astonishment, and a curse, and a reproach; and ye shall see this place no more.
The Lord hath said concerning you, O ye remnant of Judah; Go ye not into Egypt: know certainly that I have admonished you this day.

For ye dissembled in your hearts, when ye sent me unto the Lord your God, saying, Pray for us unto the Lord our God; and according unto all that the Lord our God shall say, so declare unto us, and we will do it.
And now I have this day declared it to you; but ye have not obeyed the voice of the Lord your God, nor any thing for the which he hath sent me unto you.
Now therefore know certainly that ye shall die by the sword, by the famine, and by the pestilence, in the place whither ye desire to go and to sojourn.
